analysis.one_liner: Bans making, importing, or selling asbestos-containing products, with exemptions for mining, chemical, and defense uses.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 9 Democratic sponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2008 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the nation's main toxic chemicals law to ban companies from importing, making, processing, or selling products containing asbestos, a mineral fiber that causes mesothelioma and other cancers. It would also fund a public education program about asbestos dangers and require companies to dispose of asbestos-containing stock within three years. The ban took effect two years after passage, but it carved out exemptions for existing chemical plants using asbestos, for stone and gravel products, for several mined minerals like talc, and for military and space uses certified as necessary. It is named for former Rep. Bruce Vento, who died of mesothelioma.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families exposed to asbestos at home and on the job — construction workers, mechanics, miners, and residents of towns near asbestos-contaminated sites — plus mesothelioma patients, who would get better information about research and treatment. Future generations would face less exposure to a known carcinogen.

how_it_helps.text: Bans importing, manufacturing, processing, or distributing asbestos-containing products, effective two years after enactment, with criminal penalties of up to five years in prison for knowing violations.

Directs the EPA to run a public education program warning consumers and workers about asbestos in homes and workplaces, and to connect patients and front-line health care providers with information on treatments and clinical trials.
Expands the legal definition of asbestos to include winchite, richterite, and other asbestiform amphibole minerals, closing a gap that had left some disease-causing fibers unregulated.
Requires companies holding asbestos-containing products to dispose of them within three years, and lets any citizen petition the EPA to start a rulemaking under the ban.
Bans asbestos-containing talc, vermiculite, and similar minerals outright in food, cosmetics, soaps, shampoos, drugs, garden products, and children's products, regardless of tested levels.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that import, manufacture, or sell asbestos-containing products — chemical plants, mines, and importers — which would have to test their materials, find substitutes, or petition for exemptions, and bear the cost of disposing of asbestos stock.

drawbacks.text: The ban is heavily carved up: existing chlor-alkali plants that use asbestos can continue doing so subject to periodic EPA review, taconite pellets and iron ore are fully exempt, and stone, sand, and gravel aggregates plus calcium carbonate, olivine, talc, vermiculite, and wollastonite may still be sold if they test below set asbestos levels.
Tested-below-a-threshold exemptions for minerals rely on EPA test methods that take years to establish, meaning contaminated material could keep flowing to consumers while the rules are developed.
The Defense Department and NASA can self-certify exemptions for 'critical functions' without independent EPA review, renewable every five years.
Compliance testing, written receipts for every shipment, and mandatory disposal would impose real costs on mining, aggregate, and chemical businesses, including smaller operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is large and one-directional: asbestos is a proven carcinogen with no safe level of exposure, and a ban would prevent future cases of an almost always fatal cancer. The bill's design weaknesses are in its exemptions, not its core — the chlor-alkali, taconite, and mineral carve-outs let significant exposure continue for years, and the bill leans on slow EPA rulemaking to tighten them. Still, for most households the practical benefit is real: fewer asbestos-containing products reaching homes and workplaces. The main honest cost is compliance expense for materials producers, some of it unavoidable in a transition off asbestos.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee the day it was introduced, and neither ever took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green introduced the bill on September 15, 2008, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
That same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill still sitting in committee.
The bill was introduced in the final weeks of a two-year session, leaving almost no runway even if the committee had moved quickly.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that make, import, or use asbestos-containing products — chemical plants, mines, and importers — kept operating under the pre-existing rules, which left most asbestos fibers unregulated. Household exposure to asbestos-containing products continued unabated.

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban asbestos-containing products under the Toxic Substances Control Act.

for.name: 8 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. McCollum, Solis, Capps, Baldwin, Butterfield, Schakowsky, Matsui, Cohen)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original supporters at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in its environment subcommittee from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: Asbestos-related industries
against.role: Chlor-alkali chemical plants, taconite and mineral producers, and importers of asbestos-containing products
against.what_they_did: Would have faced the ban and testing requirements; no industry lobbying on the bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; because the bill never got a hearing or vote, opposition never took a formal, recorded shape.

industries.industry: Asbestos product manufacturers, importers, and distributors
industries.note: The bill bans their products outright after a two-year phase-in, with criminal penalties for knowing violations. Their continued sales meant continued asbestos exposure for workers and households.

Existing plants using asbestos diaphragms are permanently exempt, subject only to periodic EPA review that could end the exemption. These plants turn asbestos into chlorine and caustic soda, and the exemption locks in their reliance on it.

industries.industry: Taconite and iron ore mining (Minnesota Iron Range)
industries.note: Taconite pellets and iron ore destined for pellet production are exempt from the ban entirely, locking in existing mining practice. Iron ore mining has been linked to asbestos-like fiber exposures, though the exemption does cover extraction waste.

industries.industry: Talc, vermiculite, and other mineral producers
industries.note: These minerals are exempt if they test below 0.001 percent asbestos, but the exemption is void for food, cosmetics, soaps, shampoos, drugs, garden products, and children's goods. Producers keep most markets but must fund testing and lose consumer-product uses.

industries.industry: Stone, sand, and gravel aggregate producers
industries.note: Aggregates used in cemented materials are exempt below a 0.25 percent asbestos level but must be tested and accompanied by written certifications. Their products stay on the market with added compliance cost, and construction workers keep handling material with trace asbestos.

The bill gives the Defense Department and NASA a self-certification path to keep using asbestos for 'critical functions,' renewable every five years, keeping their contractors' asbestos supply chains legal without independent health review.
